solutions.check: 32 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), agrees with the 31 answers the paper printed

clue.text: -Bob met by Victoria

parts.note: a Victoria is a well-known variety of plum
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Bob was met at Victoria station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is the weight on a plumb line; 'Victoria' looks like the London station but is the plum. 'by' just sets the two pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A plummet is the lead weight on a sounding line, the same thing as a bob.

clue.text: Those classically advised to rearm ?

parts.note: the Latin tag 'if you want peace, prepare for war' is addressed to those who desire peace

explanation.surface: People told in ancient times to take up weapons again.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman maxim si vis pacem, para bellum advises anyone wanting peace to prepare for war.
explanation.definitionFit: Peace-lovers are, by the classical maxim, the very people told to arm for war.

clue.text: Use of new suite — about £1

indicators.note: the reworked letters go about the money, enclosing it
new suggests a fresh arrangement of these letters

parts.note: L is the pound sign's letter and I is the Roman one

explanation.surface: Buying a new suite of furniture for about a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: '£1' gives two letters: L for pound (from Latin libra) and I for one; 'new' and 'about' do the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To utilise is to make use of something.

clue.text: Beaten at Hastings-about, to make changes,-it's thought

indicators.note: the word for beaten goes about the other word

parts.note: Hastings hosts a famous annual chess congress, and a player beaten there is mated
to edit is to make changes to a text

explanation.surface: Someone beaten at the Battle of Hastings reflects on making changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hastings' points to 1066, but it is the seaside town's annual chess tournament.
explanation.definitionFit: Something meditated is something thought over and considered.

clue.text: Gin makes us a bit uppish

indicators.note: in a down answer, going up means the letters are read from the bottom

parts.note: a part is a bit of something

explanation.surface: Gin makes us rather snooty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' looks like the drink but means a snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin is a snare for catching animals, a kind of trap.

clue.text: What won't go off has gone off in the heat

parts.note: a shell or firework that fails to explode is a dud

indicators.note: gone off means spoiled or turned bad, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A firework that won't explode has gone off after all in the hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What won't go off' reads as something durable but is a failed shell. 'in the' links to the definition, as in the phrase 'in high dudgeon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is a fit of angry resentment, the heat of indignation.

clue.text: Perch for two ? It sounds very low

explanation.surface: A fish big enough for two, making a deep noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The bass is a fish like the perch, so 'perch for two' is twice that fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass is a perch-like fish, so two of them; also the lowest-pitched instrument of the violin family.

clue.text: Charge one in the red

indicators.note: the numeral goes inside the word for the red

parts.note: being in the red means being in debt
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Charging someone who is overdrawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A debit is an entry charged against an account.

clue.text: I except climbing — initially very easy, if dodgy.

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means the letters go upward

parts.note: save means except, as in 'all save one'

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Apart from climbing, everything is very easy for someone who is shifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns I SAVE to read EVASI upwards; then come V and E.
explanation.definitionFit: An evasive person avoids answering directly, dodging the question.

clue.text: No child of two, only children, she

definitions.text: No child of two, only children, she

parts.words: No child of two, only children, she
parts.note: a family relation impossible when both parents had no brothers or sisters

explanation.surface: A girl who cannot be the daughter of two only children.
explanation.walkthrough: She is the daughter of a sibling, so if both parents are only children she cannot exist.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl or woman who is a brother's or sister's daughter needs a parent with siblings.

clue.text: "Sweetest Shakespeare, Fancy's ——" (Milton)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Milton's L'Allegro calls Shakespeare the offspring of imagination

explanation.surface: A line of Milton praising Shakespeare, with its last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line in Milton's poem L'Allegro is 'sweetest Shakespeare, fancy's child'; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's line names Shakespeare as the offspring of fancy, meaning imagination.

clue.text: Overshadow a stupid class

parts.note: dumb is an informal word for stupid
rate means a class or grade, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: A dim group of pupils outshone by others.
explanation.definitionFit: To adumbrate is to foreshadow or overshadow, casting a shadow over something.

clue.text: Palms off? But the hands were empty

indicators.note: the hands were holding the empty thing, so it sits inside them

parts.note: fists are closed hands
O, a zero, stands for nothing, something empty

explanation.surface: A conjuror palms something off, yet his hands were shown to be empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palms off' suggests a sleight-of-hand trick; the picture is fists with nothing (O) held inside them, the inside-them signalled by 'were'.
explanation.definitionFit: To foist something on someone is to palm it off on them deceitfully.

clue.text: Not sharp and experienced but on the level!

parts.note: in music a note that is not sharp may be flat
wise means made knowing by experience

explanation.surface: Someone neither shrewd nor seasoned, yet honest and straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the level' looks like 'honest' but means lying flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatwise means lying with the flat side down, horizontal.

clue.text: Attacks vulgar woman left and right

parts.note: broad is slang for a woman
left and right are the two sides

explanation.surface: A coarse woman attacks to the left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a forceful verbal attack, from a ship's full volley of guns.

clue.text: State of anxiety-hard hit about one point

indicators.note: the hard hit goes round the point, holding it inside

parts.note: a swat is a sharp hard blow
E, east, is one point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious after being hit hard on one spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a sweat is to be in a state of nervous worry.

clue.text: Wild bands rise with unreasoning violence

indicators.note: wild suggests these letters running out of control into a new order

explanation.surface: Unruly gangs rise up in mindless violence.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabidness is frenzied fury, like that of a mad dog, beyond all reason.

clue.text: The opposite of Lovelace's first love

definitions.text: The opposite of Lovelace's first love

parts.words: The opposite of Lovelace's first love
parts.note: Richard Lovelace wrote 'I could not love thee, dear, so much, loved I not honour more'

explanation.surface: The reverse of what a Cavalier poet loved most.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace's poem To Lucasta, Going to the Wars puts honour before his beloved; its opposite is shame.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovelace loved honour first, and the opposite of honour is shame and disgrace.

clue.text: Perhaps is rocky, with stones

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady, so these letters wobble into a new order

explanation.surface: Perhaps the ground is rocky, full of stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stones' looks like rubble but means gems.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapphires are precious blue gemstones.

clue.text: Musical time when Cleopatra loved Caesar

explanation.surface: A stage show set when the Egyptian queen loved the Roman general.
explanation.walkthrough: Salad Days is a long-running 1950s British stage musical; Shakespeare's Cleopatra calls her time with Caesar 'my salad days, when I was green in judgment'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a famous British stage show and the phrase for youthful inexperience, from Shakespeare's Cleopatra recalling her green years.

clue.text: Hit Mrs Wilcox with a plate

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or hit
Ella Wheeler Wilcox was an American poet

explanation.surface: Someone strikes Mrs Wilcox with a dinner plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamella is a thin layer or plate, as in the gills of a mushroom.

clue.text: Slush all round a county

indicators.note: the slush is placed all round the next piece, enclosing it

parts.note: slop is watery mess, like slush

explanation.surface: A county where melting snow lies all around.
explanation.walkthrough: SALOP is an old name for Shropshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Salop is the traditional abbreviated name of the English county of Shropshire.

clue.text: Mad about a forward priest of-Troy

indicators.note: the word for mad goes about the next letter

parts.note: loco is slang for mad
on means forward, as in 'go on'

explanation.surface: A mad, pushy priest in ancient Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: Laocoon was the Trojan priest who warned against the wooden horse and was killed by sea serpents.
explanation.definitionFit: Laocoon was Apollo's priest at Troy in Greek legend.

clue.text: Cat and moose imbroglio-at times-Homeric?

indicators.note: an imbroglio is a confused tangle, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A muddle of cat and moose in an epic setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on the saying 'even Homer nods': the great poet was sometimes asleep on the job.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially Homer nods, so at times he was dozing, in a deep stupor.

clue.text: County business calls for a drink

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: A county firm needs a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot drink made from cacao powder.

clue.text: Conditions in one's school days

explanation.surface: Rules laid down in someone's schooldays.
explanation.definitionFit: Terms are conditions of an agreement, and also the divisions of the school year.

clue.text: Semitic idol-fond of children ?

explanation.surface: An ancient god of the Semites who loved little ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is ironic: children were sacrificed to this god.
explanation.definitionFit: Moloch was a Canaanite deity to whom children were offered, so fond of them in a grim sense.

clue.text: —— of day. Overture to dawn chorus?

explanation.surface: The first light, and the first bird call of morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peep of day' is dawn; a peep is also a bird's tiny cheep, a fitting opener to the birds' morning song.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase for first daylight, and a small chirping sound like that of a young bird.

clue.text: Taylor's poetical follower, musical forerunner

explanation.surface: Someone who came after a poet called Taylor and before a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet was Samuel Taylor Coleridge, where the name follows Taylor; the composer was Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, where it comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname follows 'Taylor' in the Romantic poet's full name and precedes it in the composer's hyphenated surname.

clue.text: Suffice it's in our favour

indicators.note: the word for suffice goes inside the other word

parts.note: to do is to suffice, as in 'that will do'

explanation.surface: Enough to say it works to our advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from 'in good odour', meaning in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: Odour means reputation or standing, as in being in good odour with someone, in their favour.

clue.text: Collects a plentiful supply.

parts.note: masses means a great abundance

explanation.surface: Someone gathering an abundant stock.
explanation.definitionFit: To amass is to gather or accumulate, to collect.

clue.text: Annual payments, for our authors?

parts.note: PA, per annum, means yearly
rents are regular payments

explanation.surface: Yearly royalties paid to writers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'authors' looks literary, but our parents authored us.
explanation.definitionFit: Fathers and mothers are those who brought us into being, our originators.
